config.title: Error Boundary

intro.title: Error Boundary
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a React component called an Error Boundary to catch and handle JavaScript errors anywhere in your component tree. You will learn the core concept of error boundaries, which are special React components that use lifecycle methods to detect errors in their child components and display a fallback UI instead of crashing the entire app. The main technologies involved are React, TypeScript, and class components with the `componentDidCatch` lifecycle method. By the end, you'll create a reusable error boundary that gracefully manages errors and improves user experience in your applications.
intro.usecase: Error Boundaries are essential in production React applications to prevent a single component failure from crashing an entire user interface. For example, in a complex dashboard with multiple independent data panels—like charts, tables, and status widgets—an error in one panel's data fetching can be gracefully contained, allowing the rest of the dashboard to remain functional. Similarly, in a large e-commerce product page, an error in a recommendation carousel or review section should not break the core 'Add to Cart' functionality or main product display. Implementing Error Boundaries ensures a resilient user experience by isolating failures and displaying fallback UI, which is a standard practice in professional frontend development.

objectives: Implement a class component that extends React's ErrorBoundary
Configure the componentDidCatch lifecycle method to handle errors
Render fallback UI when an error is caught
Initialize state to track error status and error details
Integrate the Error Boundary component into a component tree
Manipulate component behavior to demonstrate error boundaries in action
Apply error boundaries to prevent application crashes from component errors

steps.title: Define ErrorBoundary component with TypeScript interface
steps.instruction: Create a class component called ErrorBoundary that extends React.Component. Use TypeScript generics to define props and state interfaces: props should be an empty object, state should have an 'hasError' boolean property.
steps.hint: Use 'class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component<{}, { hasError: boolean }>' to define the component with TypeScript types.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { Component, ErrorInfo } from 'react';

// Create the ErrorBoundary class component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A class component named ErrorBoundary is defined with proper TypeScript generics for props and state.
successCriteria: ErrorBoundary component exists as a class extending React.Component with generic types <{}, { hasError: boolean }>
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but check the TypeScript generics. The props should be empty object {} and state should have 'hasError: boolean'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Make sure it's a class component named ErrorBoundary that extends React.Component with TypeScript generics.

steps.title: Define ErrorBoundary state interface
steps.instruction: Inside the ErrorBoundary class component, define a TypeScript interface named ErrorBoundaryState with two properties: hasError (boolean) and errorMessage (string).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions. Remember to specify types for each property.
steps.expectedOutcome: An interface named ErrorBoundaryState is created with the correct property types.
successCriteria: The ErrorBoundaryState interface is defined with hasError: boolean and errorMessage: string properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined an interface, but check that it has both required properties with correct types: hasError (boolean) and errorMessage (string).
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Make sure to define ErrorBoundaryState with both properties and their types.

steps.title: Initialize ErrorBoundary state in constructor
steps.instruction: Add a constructor to the ErrorBoundary class component and initialize the state with hasError: false and errorMessage: ''
steps.hint: In TypeScript class components, the constructor receives props as the first parameter and must call super(props). Then set this.state to the initial state object.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now has a constructor that properly initializes the component state with the required default values.
successCriteria: The ErrorBoundary class has a constructor that calls super(props) and sets this.state to { hasError: false, errorMessage: '' }
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your constructor calls super(props) and sets this.state to exactly { hasError: false, errorMessage: '' }.
steps.feedbackWrong: The constructor should initialize the state with hasError: false and errorMessage: ''. Remember to call super(props) first.

steps.title: Implement getDerivedStateFromError lifecycle method
steps.instruction: Inside the ErrorBoundary class, add a static method named getDerivedStateFromError that takes an error parameter and returns an object with hasError set to true and errorMessage set to error.message.
steps.hint: This static method should be placed inside the class but outside the constructor. It receives an error object and must return the new state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary class now has a static getDerivedStateFromError method that updates state when an error occurs in child components.
successCriteria: The ErrorBoundary class contains a static getDerivedStateFromError method that returns { hasError: true, errorMessage: error.message }.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure getDerivedStateFromError is a static method that takes an error parameter and returns an object with hasError: true and errorMessage set to error.message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The getDerivedStateFromError method is missing or incorrect. It should be a static method that returns state with hasError: true and errorMessage from the error parameter.

steps.title: Implement componentDidCatch lifecycle method
steps.instruction: Add the componentDidCatch lifecycle method to your ErrorBoundary class. This method should log the error and errorInfo to the console.
steps.hint: The componentDidCatch method receives two parameters: error and errorInfo. Use console.log to output both values.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now has a componentDidCatch method that logs errors to the console.
successCriteria: componentDidCatch method is implemented with error and errorInfo parameters, and logs both values to console
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your componentDidCatch method accepts both error and errorInfo parameters and logs them to the console using console.log().
steps.feedbackWrong: The componentDidCatch method is missing or incomplete. Remember to add this lifecycle method to your ErrorBoundary class with the correct parameters and console logging.

steps.title: Create render method with conditional logic
steps.instruction: Inside the ErrorBoundary class, add a render method that conditionally returns children when no error exists, or returns error UI when hasError is true.
steps.hint: Use the state property hasError to decide what to render. When hasError is true, return an error message; otherwise, return this.props.children.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now has a render method that uses conditional logic to either show children or an error UI.
successCriteria: The render method is defined, checks this.state.hasError, returns this.props.children when false, and returns an error message element when true.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a render method, but it might not correctly handle both cases. Make sure to check this.state.hasError and return appropriate JSX for both true and false conditions.
steps.feedbackWrong: The render method is missing or doesn't properly implement conditional rendering. Check that you're using this.state.hasError to decide what to return.

steps.instruction: In the ErrorBoundary's render method, add a button element inside the error UI that, when clicked, resets the error state by setting hasError to false.

steps.expectedOutcome: The error UI now includes a button that allows the user to reset the error state and try again.
